parts.article:
Keeping Healthy at Work

(A) Being a responsible employer in New Zealand used to require a fairly short checklist: a regular salary or wages, a safe working environment, and that was about it. But these days, the checklist is growing, and companies are increasingly expected to play a much greater role in the health and wellbeing of their employees. Definitions of workplace wellness or wellbeing vary, but the World Health Organisation's definition extends the employer's responsibilities beyond safety concerns and into the wider workplace environment. Today, this means things like the boss making sure their staff aren't bored or feeling undervalued, and company trying to minimise the pressure and tensions that are experienced in the workplace. It could also involve providing 'wellness programmes' that consider all these factors and help staff to lead healthier lifestyles.

(B) This approach has found some support among employers in New Zealand. The organisation Business NZ conducted research in 2013 that found that 9 out of 10 businesses believed employee wellbeing and contentment was either desirable or a priority. It was also found that 61% of New Zealand companies with more than 100 employees now have a wellness programme. Others may join in since the Health and Safety at Work Act came into being. The emphasis of the law is still on preventing physical injury at work, but a spokesperson says that a significant focus is now also the need for employers to take an active role in the wider health and wellbeing of staff.

(C) Kelly Davis Martin is the director of Achieve Wellness, which helps companies set up wellness programmes. She says the increase in companies looking to set up programmes is positive, but she would like to see a lot more being done. ‘We need to make sure these programmes are worthwhile and contribute to real change,’ she says. This is supported by data from the Productivity Commission, which shows that New Zealanders work as hard as employees in other western countries, but produce less. This means that they need to work smarter, not harder, and wellness programmes might help with that.

(D) Insurance provider Accident Compensation Corporation is one New Zealand organisation that has recently set up a wellness programme. The first initiative involves the 2,000 staff taking part in a special challenge, where teams compete with each other to see who can walk the furthest in a week. A spokesperson says there is no single reason behind the programme, except that it is an essential part of keeping staff healthy. Phone company 2degrees Mobile also began its first wellness programme recently. Manager Sarah Friis says the company was looking to increase staff engagement and show employees they were of value. The company has close to 800 employees, and its programme was established by eight volunteers from around the business. A range of initiatives were included in the programme, such as sports events and team challenges, and vaccinations were offered against things like influenza for which there was no charge. This year 2degrees has taken professional advice, but Friis says their programme is still internally run because this is vital to keeping the energy going and getting feedback on what is working and what needs to changed. It now has an online facility which allows employees to keep up to date with all the latest advice on health and wellness. Two years in, Friis says one of the obvious benefits is a sense of greater unity, which she believes has been achieved by all staff eating a healthy lunch as a group every now and again. A more measurable benefit was shown in the 2degrees staff survey, which the company conducts every year, showing that more staff now recognise that 2degrees cares about the wellness of its employees.

(E) One further New Zealand company that is developing its wellness programme is Sovereign Insurance. CEO Symon Brewis-Weston says that when he started at the company, the existing programme was satisfactory, with a number of employees using the opportunity to receive counselling. But he wanted more people to become involved and decided to include activities that created more staff interest. So the new scheme offers financial contributions for employee sports’ teams and discounts on the likes of dental treatment. The company also has quarterly wellbeing challenges, including one where staff cut down on sugar and got tips on ways to reduce their daily intake. About 50% of staff took part, says Brewis-Weston.

(F) Interestingly, however, some research from the USA, where wellness programmes have been in place much longer, suggests that the initiatives are not always as impressive as you might think. One study suggests that participants lost an average of less than half a kilogram a year, and that there were no significant reductions in the costs involved when it is necessary for employees to go to hospital for care. Meanwhile, the US book Surviving Workplace Wellness suggests that done badly, the programmes waste money and upset staff who feel they are made to take too many unnecessary tests. Given these findings, New Zealand companies will have to work hard to make sure their own wellness programmes achieve more success.

questions.question: New Zealand has a better workplace safety record than many other countries.

analyses.content: 文章首句虽然提到了新西兰的安全工作环境，但全文根本没有把新西兰和“许多其他国家”的职场安全记录做任何比较。
你可能会在后续段落看到“other western countries”，但千万别自己脑补出安全记录的对比，没比过就是NOT GIVEN。

(A) Being a responsible employer in New Zealand used to require a fairly short checklist: a regular salary or wages, a safe working environment, and that was about it. But these days, the checklist is growing, and companies are increasingly expected to play a much greater role in the health and wellbeing of their employees.

questions.question: According to the World Health Organisation, companies today should be responsible for reducing workers’ stress.

analyses.content: 世卫组织认为现在的雇主责任包括要尽量减少员工在职场中感到的压力和紧张情绪，这完全对应题目里的“减轻员工压力”。
如果你没看出“minimise the pressure and tensions”就是“reducing workers’ stress”的直接替换，就容易找错定位。

Definitions of workplace wellness or wellbeing vary, but the World Health Organisation's definition extends the employer's responsibilities beyond safety concerns and into the wider workplace environment. Today, this means things like the boss making sure their staff aren't bored or feeling undervalued, and company trying to minimise the pressure and tensions that are experienced in the workplace.

questions.question: Business NZ research showed that most companies want their employees to feel positive about their work.

analyses.content: Business NZ的研究直接指出十分之九（即绝大多数）的企业认为员工的幸福感和满足感是值得追求的优先事项。
The organisation Business NZ conducted research in 2013 that found that 9 out of 10 businesses believed employee wellbeing and contentment was either desirable or a priority.

questions.question: Kelly Davis Martin thinks companies today are doing enough to promote workers’ wellness.

analyses.content: Kelly明确表示她希望能看到公司“采取更多的行动”，这说明她觉得目前公司做得还不够。
你可能会看到前半句的“positive”就以为她是完全认可的，但做判断题一定要盯紧转折词“but”后面的核心观点。

She says the increase in companies looking to set up programmes is positive, but she would like to see a lot more being done. ‘We need to make sure these programmes are worthwhile and contribute to real change,’ she says.

questions.question: Productivity Commission data shows New Zealanders should be working more hours.

analyses.content: 生产力委员会的数据和结论是，新西兰人需要的是“更聪明地工作，而不是更努力地工作”，直接否定了题目中“应该工作更长时间”的说法。

This is supported by data from the Productivity Commission, which shows that New Zealanders work as hard as employees in other western countries, but produce less. This means that they need to work smarter, not harder, and wellness programmes might help with that.
